result.verdict: Not ready for a non-technical recipient. The ready state is visually striking and the Download path is obvious, but every failure state is a dead end with no recovery action, error copy is largely interchangeable and misleading, and key facts — file size, expiry, sender, trust — are presented in machine terms or omitted entirely. On large screens the card is stranded at the top above a majority-empty page.

findings.element: Dark readout body 'Ask the sender for the complete link, including everything after the # symbol.' — no key-paste field
findings.problem: Total dead end. The one fixable cause — a truncated link / lost fragment — cannot be fixed here. A recipient who has the key separately, or whose messenger stripped the fragment, has no way to paste a key or a complete link and retry; they must abandon the page.
findings.norm: Error states must offer a recovery path proportional to the cause (NN/g error-message guidelines: help users recover, provide a way forward), especially for a no-sign-in page with no other navigation.
findings.fix: Add a paste field: 'Paste the missing key, or the full link you were sent' with an 'Open file' button that re-reads the fragment and retries decryption in-page.

findings.element: Dark readout body 'Ask the sender for the complete link…' and empty sled slot below it
findings.problem: Same dead end as missing-key, and less excusable: the key was present but wrong, so the file is right there and only the credential is bad. There is no retry, no paste-a-correct-key field, and no guidance that re-clicking the original message link (rather than a forwarded copy) usually fixes it.
findings.norm: Recoverable input errors must be correctable in place without restarting the flow; a wrong credential should behave like a wrong password — re-enter and retry.
findings.fix: Provide the same paste-key / paste-full-link field with retry, plus one line: 'If you were forwarded this link, try the original message instead.'

findings.element: Sled slot under the dark readout in missing-key, expired, revoked and not-found states (empty metallic bar)
findings.problem: In the ready state this exact slot holds the orange Download button; in every error state it is an empty silver bar. It reads as a disabled button, a stalled progress bar, or a scrollbar — users will tap/click it and get nothing. The page's only action affordance is a fake one.
findings.norm: Affordance consistency: an element's form must not promise interactivity it doesn't have; primary CTA position must either hold a real action or be removed.
findings.fix: Put a real action in the slot: 'Copy a message to the sender' (pre-written request for a new/complete link) in every error state, or collapse the empty slot entirely.

findings.element: Body copy 'Ask the sender for a new share link. Your files have not been changed.' — identical in expired, revoked and not-found
findings.problem: Three different causes get one identical paragraph, so the recipient learns nothing about what happened or how likely a new link is to fix it. Worse, 'Your files have not been changed' is sender-centric nonsense for a recipient: they have no files here, and it raises the unasked fear that files might have been changed or deleted. Revoked (a deliberate act by the sender) and not-found (likely a mistyped/truncated link) need materially different explanations.
findings.norm: Error copy must name the specific cause, its consequence for this user, and the specific next step; boilerplate shared across causes fails all three.
findings.fix: Differentiate: Expired — 'This link stopped working on [date]. The file itself is fine — ask [sender] for a fresh link.' Revoked — 'The sender turned this link off. Only they can share it again.' Not found — 'This link doesn't match any shared file — it may be incomplete. Check you opened the whole link, then ask the sender to resend it.' Delete 'Your files have not been changed' everywhere.

findings.element: White label reused for error titles: 'Share link expired', 'Share link revoked', 'Share link not found', 'This link is missing a valid decryption key'
findings.problem: The white label is the filename slot in the ready state. Error titles rendered in the same slot, same type, are initially parseable as filenames ('share-link-expired' could be a file), and nothing — no icon, no error colour, no 'Couldn't open this file' framing — marks them as errors. The only state signal is the LED turning grey, which no first-time user will decode.
findings.norm: Category convention (Drive, Dropbox, WeTransfer): unavailable-file pages lead with an unmistakable status (icon + plain heading) visually distinct from file metadata.
findings.fix: Add a distinct error treatment: an ✕/clock icon in signal orange-red beside the title, a small status line above the label (e.g. 'This link no longer works'), keeping the label reserved for actual filenames.

findings.element: Readout 'TRANSFER SIZE / 48,254 encrypted bytes' (and '3,041 encrypted bytes' on mobile)
findings.problem: Bytes with thousands separators is the least human unit available, and 'encrypted bytes' is meaningless jargon — a non-technical recipient cannot judge whether this is a photo or a movie, or whether it will fit on their phone. It is also the encrypted size, not the size of the file they will actually receive.
findings.norm: Every consumer file surface (Drive, Dropbox, WeTransfer, OS file managers) shows human units (KB/MB/GB) of the delivered file.
findings.fix: Show '47 KB' (the decrypted file size) as the readout; if encrypted size is technically interesting, demote it to a tooltip or omit it.

findings.element: Readout 'LINK EXPIRES / 11/11/2026, 4:55:49 PM'
findings.problem: Three failures in one line: second-level precision implies a live countdown that isn't happening; 11/11 is ambiguous or at least unscannable outside the US and no timezone is given, so 'when does this stop working?' is unanswerable; and there is no relative phrasing ('in 6 days') and no urgency treatment if expiry is near. On mobile the line is one of only two facts given and neither helps the user act in time.
findings.norm: Show relative time first ('Expires in 6 days'), absolute date on the user's locale without seconds ('11 Nov 2026, 4:55 PM'), and warn explicitly when under 24 hours remain.
findings.fix: Render 'Expires in 6 days · 11 Nov 2026, 4:55 PM' and, when <24h, an orange 'Expires today' treatment.

findings.element: Whole page: filename + size + expiry only — no sender, no file type, no trust cue
findings.problem: A stranger (or an AI agent) sent this person an encrypted file to download from an unfamiliar brand. The page gives no sender name, no file-type icon/preview, and no 'only download files you were expecting' guidance. That is both a usability gap (is this the file I was promised?) and a phishing-shaped hole: the design trains recipients to click Download on any branded link.
findings.norm: Share-recipient pages (Google Drive, Dropbox) foreground who shared the item and what it is before the download action.
findings.fix: Add sender identity wherever the link carries it ('Shared by …'), a large file-type glyph next to the filename, and one muted line: 'Only download this if you were expecting a file from the sender.'

findings.element: Readout 'Checking this share link…' with orange LED and thin grey slot bar
findings.problem: Loading is expressed only by static text. The grey slot bar shows no fill, there is no spinner or pulsing LED, no elapsed feedback, and no timeout/retry or cancel if the check hangs — on a slow connection this is indistinguishable from a frozen page. The LED is a dimmer orange than the ready state's glowing orange, a distinction without a legend.
findings.norm: Indeterminate operations need visible motion within ~1s and a failure/timeout path; static 'Checking…' text reads as stalled.
findings.fix: Animate the LED/readout (pulse or ellipsis), add an indeterminate progress shimmer in the slot, and after ~10s show 'Still checking — Retry' with a working retry control.

findings.element: Small grey-on-dark labels 'TRANSFER SIZE' / 'LINK EXPIRES' and grey readout body text; footer 'Client-side encryption. The key stays in your browser.'
findings.problem: The supporting text sits at contrast levels a first-time or low-vision user will struggle with: tiny letter-spaced grey labels on near-black, pale beige body copy in the error readouts on dark brown-black, and mid-grey monospace on the light dotted ground below the chassis. The most reassurance-critical line on the page (the footer) is among the least legible.
findings.norm: WCAG 2.1 AA: 4.5:1 for body text, 3:1 minimum for large text; small caps labels need more, not less, contrast than body copy.
findings.fix: Raise label and body colours to ≥4.5:1 against their backgrounds (verify orange readout and beige error text with a checker), darken the footer text, and increase footer/label font size by 1–2px.

findings.element: Reassurance copy pair: chassis line 'Your browser decrypts this file. No sign-in required.' and page footer 'Client-side encryption. The key stays in your browser.'
findings.problem: The same idea is stated twice, once well and once in jargon the persona cannot parse ('client-side', 'key'). The jargon version is given the permanent footer slot on every state — including error states where 'the key stays in your browser' is actively unhelpful (the problem is the key/link). Meanwhile 'No sign-in required', the most useful reassurance, appears only in the ready state and vanishes exactly when an anxious user hits an error.
findings.norm: One plain-language reassurance, repeated consistently; supporting copy should respond to the user's current state, not recite a security architecture slogan.
findings.fix: Keep 'Your browser decrypts this file. No sign-in required.' as the single chassis line on all states; replace the footer with state-relevant help ('Sent a broken link? Ask the sender to copy the full link from their share screen.') or remove it.

findings.element: Page layout: logo + single chassis card occupying roughly the top 40% of the viewport
findings.problem: At 1440×900 and especially 1920×1080 the card is anchored near the top and the remaining ~55–65% of the screen is empty dotted background. The page reads as unfinished or as if content failed to load below the fold — a real risk for a user already unsure whether the link worked. Nothing is vertically centred and nothing scales with the larger canvas.
findings.norm: Single-card task pages centre the card in the viewport at all sizes; whitespace should frame the task, not abandon it.
findings.fix: Vertically centre the logo+card group (or anchor at ~40% viewport height), cap chassis width as now, and let the dotted ground fill the rest symmetrically.

findings.element: 'Agent Drive' wordmark position
findings.problem: The logo is neither a page header (not at a corner or full-width bar) nor centred over the card — it is left-aligned to the card's edge, floating mid-screen at desktop widths. It looks like a layout bug, weakens the brand-as-trust-signal role, and gives the eye no stable starting point.
findings.norm: A lone brand mark on a task page is either a conventional top-left header or centred above the card it authenticates.
findings.fix: Centre the wordmark above the chassis (matching the card's centre axis), or move it to a true top-left header position consistently across viewports.

findings.element: White filename label with 5-line filename 'a-very-long-synthetic-file-name-for-wrapping-checks-2026-board-meeting-minutes-final-v7-reviewed-by-everyone.txt'
findings.problem: Good news: it wraps instead of overflowing. Bad news: the label triples in height, becomes the dominant element on the page, pushes the readouts and Download down, and gives no file-type icon to aid scanning. Middle-elision or a 2-line clamp with the extension preserved would communicate the same identity at a third of the vertical cost, keeping Download in the first screenful on shorter phones.
findings.norm: File lists truncate long names (ideally middle-truncate, always preserving extension) with full name available on tap/long-press.
findings.fix: Clamp the label to 2 lines with middle truncation ('a-very-long-synthetic-…-by-everyone.txt'), add a file-type glyph, and expose the full name via tap tooltip.

findings.element: Footer 'Client-side encryption. The key stays in your browser.' on 375px viewport
findings.problem: The line wraps to two lines and centre-aligns with an orphaned 'browser.' under a ragged first line, sitting detached below the chassis shadow. Combined with the long-filename state, the mobile page's vertical rhythm — label, readouts, button, two stray text lines — feels accidental rather than set.
findings.norm: Auxiliary lines on mobile should be width-constrained to the card, left- or centre-aligned with a balanced wrap, and spaced as part of the card group.
findings.fix: Constrain footer width to the chassis, allow a balanced 2-line wrap, and tighten its offset from the chassis so it reads as part of the unit.

findings.element: State signalling: LED (glowing orange / flat orange / grey) + 'ENCRYPTED FILE TRANSFER' header + tick-strip decoration
findings.problem: State is encoded almost entirely by one 8px dot whose three appearances (glow, flat, grey) have no labels and no legend — the difference between 'loading' and 'ready', and between 'error' and 'off', is invisible to anyone who doesn't already know the hardware metaphor. The tick strip to the right of the header is pure noise occupying the header's right half, competing with nothing but signalling nothing. The Rack metaphor is being spent on decoration instead of communication.
findings.norm: Status must never be carried by colour alone (WCAG 1.4.1); pair every state with an icon or word.
findings.fix: Add a text status next to the LED ('Ready', 'Checking…', 'Link problem') and keep colour as reinforcement; drop or shrink the decorative tick strip.

findings.element: Primary button 'Download'
findings.problem: The button is excellent in prominence but underspecified: no download icon, no file size on the button, and no shown 'decrypting/downloading' or completed state anywhere in the set — for a browser-decrypted file the wait after clicking is exactly where a non-technical user needs feedback ('Preparing your file…', then the save prompt explanation). As shown, a click that takes seconds to decrypt will look like nothing happened.
findings.norm: Primary actions that trigger non-instant work show an in-button progress state and a completion cue.
findings.fix: On click, switch the button to 'Decrypting…' with progress, then 'Saved — check your downloads' with a 'Download again' secondary action.

findings.element: Dark readout panel height across states
findings.problem: The readout window is tall in missing-key, shorter in expired/revoked/not-found, and medium in loading — the chassis visibly breathes between states for no content reason. If a recipient reloads or the sender watches over their shoulder, the shifting geometry undermines the solid-hardware metaphor and can shift the slot bar under the user's cursor.
findings.norm: Fixed component geometry across states; content changes inside a stable frame (no layout shift).
findings.fix: Fix the readout to one height for all states; vertically centre shorter messages within it.

excellent: 1440x900-ready.png — the orange 'Download' button: full sled width, single accent colour, unambiguous primary action; this is exactly right for the persona and carries over well to 375x812-ready-longname.png as a generous touch target.

1440x900-missing-key.png — the sentence 'Ask the sender for the complete link, including everything after the # symbol' correctly diagnoses the most common real-world cause (fragment stripped in transit) in near-plain language; the concept is right, it just needs a recovery control attached.

1440x900-ready.png — 'Your browser decrypts this file. No sign-in required.' placed directly under the Download button answers the two biggest first-time anxieties (privacy, account wall) at the point of action.

375x812-ready-longname.png — the extreme filename wraps cleanly inside the white label with no overflow, clipping or horizontal scroll on a 375px viewport; the chassis itself fits the mobile width comfortably on both mobile screenshots.

result.verdict: The 'Rack' hardware aesthetic is distinctive and memorable, and the happy-path card fits cleanly on desktop and mobile—Even with a 108-character filename. However, the page fails its core non-technical recipient persona in error and edge states: it tells recipients 'Your files have not been changed' (copy meant for a file owner, not a downloader), strands users with truncated '#key' links at a dead end without a key input, leaves a broken-looking 6px empty grey slot where the Download button was, and uses raw 'encrypted bytes' and duplicate encryption footers.

findings.element: Dark readout window body copy in Expired, Revoked, and Not Found states ('Ask the sender for a new share link. Your files have not been changed.')
findings.problem: All three server-side error states say 'Your files have not been changed.' The user on this page is an unauthenticated recipient trying to download someone else's file—they do not have 'Your files' stored here. To a non-technical recipient, this reads either as broken sender-facing copy or an alarming message implying the link might have altered files on their own device. Additionally, Expired, Revoked, and Not Found all use identical boilerplate instead of explaining why the link failed.
findings.norm: Error messages must address the actual user role (recipient) and clearly distinguish between a link passing its expiration date, a sender intentionally revoking access, and a mistyped/non-existent URL.
findings.fix: Remove 'Your files have not been changed.' Tailor the explanation to each state for a recipient: Expired -> 'This link has passed its expiration date. Ask the sender for a new link.'; Revoked -> 'The sender turned off access to this link. Contact them if you still need the file.'; Not Found -> 'Check that the link wasn't cut off when copied, or ask the sender for a new link.'

findings.element: Missing key and Wrong key states (readout window and bottom action slot)
findings.problem: URL fragments (#key) are frequently stripped or wrapped across lines by email clients, enterprise link scanners, and chat apps. When the key is missing or incomplete, the UI hits a hard dead end ('Ask the sender for the complete link...') with no way for the recipient to paste the missing key or the full unsplit URL they already have in their email/message.
findings.norm: Zero-knowledge file-sharing apps (e.g., Tresorit Send, Proton Drive, Bitwarden Send) provide an inline input field to paste the decryption key or full link when the URL fragment is missing or corrupted, enabling immediate self-recovery.
findings.fix: Add a compact input field and 'Unlock file' button inside the sled when the key is missing or invalid so the recipient can paste the full link or the part after '#' without contacting the sender.

findings.element: Empty 6px grey horizontal bar at the bottom of the dark sled in Loading and all Error states
findings.problem: In every state where the orange 'Download' button is absent (Loading, Missing Key, Wrong Key, Expired, Revoked, Not Found), a thin ~6px recessed grey bar sits at the bottom of the dark sled. It looks like an unstyled empty container, a stuck 0% progress bar, or a broken scrollbar.
findings.norm: Conditional action slots should either collapse cleanly with consistent padding, render an explicit disabled/secondary action button, or act as a clearly animated progress bar only during active loading.
findings.fix: Remove the empty grey slot in error states so the dark readout window sits cleanly inside the sled bezel, and in the loading state either animate the bar as an indeterminate progress indicator or remove it.

findings.element: TRANSFER SIZE readout ('48,254 encrypted bytes' / '3,041 encrypted bytes')
findings.problem: Displaying raw byte counts alongside technical jargon ('48,254 encrypted bytes') confuses non-technical recipients. Users cannot easily gauge whether a file is small or huge from raw bytes, and the phrase 'encrypted bytes' makes non-technical users wonder if the downloaded file will still be encrypted and unreadable on their computer.
findings.norm: Consumer-facing file download pages display human-readable file sizes (KB, MB, GB) and label the metric simply as 'FILE SIZE'.
findings.fix: Change the label from 'TRANSFER SIZE' to 'FILE SIZE' and format the value in human-readable units (e.g., '47.1 KB' and '3.0 KB').

findings.element: Chassis bottom bezel note ('Your browser decrypts this file. No sign-in required.') and external footer ('Client-side encryption. The key stays in your browser.')
findings.problem: In the Ready state, two separate grey captions sit 28px apart at the bottom of the card communicating the exact same concept twice—once in plain English inside the chassis lip, and once in technical jargon ('Client-side encryption') below the chassis. In Loading and Error states, the chassis lip note disappears, causing the bottom chassis bezel to shrink abruptly.
findings.norm: Avoid redundant trust microcopy stacked back-to-back; pick one clear, plain-language explanation and keep the hardware chassis geometry consistent across states.
findings.fix: Delete the external 'Client-side encryption. The key stays in your browser.' caption completely, and keep a single plain-language reassurance ('Decrypted privately in your browser · No sign-in required') in a consistent position.

findings.element: White filename label slot and dark readout window in Error states
findings.problem: The hardware metaphor establishes the white strip as a physical adhesive label for the filename and the dark screen below as the electronic status readout. In error states, this semantics is inverted: the error status ('Share link expired') is printed on the white filename label, while the dark readout screen holds tiny (~12px), low-contrast grey text floating inside a large empty black box with no visual status emphasis.
findings.norm: Maintain consistent component semantics and visual hierarchy: primary status alerts in a readout display should have strong contrast and clear typographic prominence, not look like muted secondary footnotes.
findings.fix: Increase the font size and contrast of the guidance text inside the dark readout window (e.g., 14–15px at ≥80% white opacity) and reduce the empty vertical dead space inside the readout box.

findings.element: LINK EXPIRES timestamp ('11/11/2026, 4:55:49 PM')
findings.problem: The expiration timestamp appears to be an unformatted JavaScript `toLocaleString()` output: it uses an ambiguous numeric month/day format (`11/11/2026`), includes noisy seconds (`:49`), and omits the timezone or relative time remaining.
findings.norm: Timestamps for non-technical users should use unambiguous month names, omit seconds, and include relative time or local timezone context.
findings.fix: Format the expiry with an unambiguous date and no seconds (e.g., 'Nov 11, 2026 at 4:55 PM' or 'In 6 days · Nov 11, 4:55 PM').

findings.element: Page vertical alignment across desktop and tablet viewports
findings.problem: The brand header and rack card are anchored near the top of the viewport (~36px from the top edge), leaving 60–70% of the screen below the card completely empty on 1440x900, 1920x1080, and 768x1024 viewports. This makes the page feel vertically unbalanced and unfinished.
findings.norm: Single-purpose utility cards (like WeTransfer, Dropbox Transfer, or login/download modals) should be optically centered in the viewport (roughly 35–45% from top) on desktop and tablet screens.
findings.fix: Vertically center the header + rack assembly within the viewport on tablet and desktop screens (using `min-height: 100dvh` flex/grid centering with a slight upward optical offset).

findings.element: Wrong Key vs. Missing Key guidance text ('Ask the sender for the complete link, including everything after the # symbol.')
findings.problem: The Wrong Key state (`375x812-wrong-key.png`) uses the exact same instruction as Missing Key, without acknowledging that a key was present in the link but didn't match the file (for instance, because extra characters were appended or the key was partially truncated).
findings.norm: Distinct error states should explain the specific failure cause so the user knows how to fix it.
findings.fix: In the Wrong Key state, clarify: 'The decryption key at the end of this link appears incomplete or modified. Check that the full text after # matches what the sender shared.'

findings.element: Primary 'Download' button and file type cue
findings.problem: The large orange Download button contains only plain text ('Download') with no download icon and no indication that clicking it both decrypts and saves the file, nor is there a download-in-progress state shown for large files.
findings.norm: Primary download CTAs benefit from a clear download icon alongside the label to reinforce immediate actionability for first-time visitors.
findings.fix: Add a crisp download arrow icon to the left of the 'Download' label (or 'Download file').

excellent: Long filename wrapping (`375x812-ready-longname.png`): The white label container expands gracefully across 5 lines on a 375px mobile screen without horizontal overflow, ugly ellipsis truncation of the `.txt` extension, or breaking the rack chassis layout.

Industrial design execution (`1440x900-ready.png`): The tactile Teenage Engineering / Braun-inspired 'Rack' chassis, ventilation ticks, glowing orange LED, recessed dark sled, and high-contrast monospace readouts create a cohesive, high-craft aesthetic.

Single-screen mobile ergonomics (`375x812-ready-longname.png`, `375x812-wrong-key.png`): The entire interface fits comfortably above the fold on a 375x812 viewport with generous touch target sizing on the primary Download button.
